travelAdvisory.summary: Exercise increased caution in Thailand due to risk of unrest. Some areas have increased risk. Violent crime is rare against tourists but does occur.

travelAdvisoryUK.summary: Most visits to Thailand are trouble-free. Be aware of the risk of street crime and scams.

healthcare.costForTourists: Private hospitals cater to medical tourists and are excellent quality. Clinic visit $30-80. Emergency room $100-500. Private hospital stay $150-500/night. Bumrungrad International Hospital (Bangkok) is world-class. Public hospitals are cheaper ($10-50) but crowded with long waits and limited English.
healthcare.pharmacyAccess: Pharmacies are everywhere and many medications available OTC that require prescriptions in Western countries — including some antibiotics and pain medications. Pharmacists often speak basic English.
healthcare.hospitalNotes: Bangkok has world-class private hospitals (Bumrungrad, Bangkok Hospital, Samitivej) popular with medical tourists. Outside Bangkok, quality drops significantly. Chiang Mai has adequate private hospitals. Islands and rural areas have very limited medical facilities — serious cases require evacuation to Bangkok.
healthcare.insuranceAdvice: Travel insurance essential. Private hospitals require proof of insurance or cash deposit upfront ($500-2,000). Medevac coverage strongly recommended if visiting islands or rural areas.

medications.generalAdvice: Thailand has extremely strict drug laws — penalties for trafficking include the death penalty. Always carry medications in original packaging with prescription labels. Bring a doctor's letter for any controlled substance. Do not buy controlled medications from Thai pharmacies without a local prescription.

scams.name: Grand Palace 'closed today' scam
scams.description: Tuk-tuk drivers or friendly strangers near the Grand Palace tell you it's closed for a 'special ceremony.' They offer to take you to a 'better' temple, then route you through gem shops and tailors who pay them commission.
scams.avoidance: Ignore anyone who tells you an attraction is closed. Walk to the entrance yourself and check. The Grand Palace is rarely closed.

scams.name: Jet ski damage scam
scams.description: Jet ski operators claim you damaged the jet ski and demand $500-2,000 for 'repairs' to pre-existing damage. They may become aggressive or threaten police.
scams.avoidance: Take photos/video of the jet ski from all angles before renting. Better yet, avoid jet ski rentals at beach resorts entirely.

scams.name: Tuk-tuk overcharging / gem shop routing
scams.description: Tuk-tuk drivers offer impossibly cheap rides (20 baht) but take you on detours through gem shops, tailors, and travel agencies. You're pressured to buy while the driver earns commission.
scams.avoidance: Use Grab (ride-hailing app) or metered taxis instead. If using a tuk-tuk, agree on fare and destination in advance. Refuse any 'special stops.'

scams.name: Ping pong show bait and switch
scams.description: Touts offer free entry to shows, then present a bill of 3,000-10,000 baht per person for drinks you didn't order. Bouncers prevent you from leaving.
scams.avoidance: Avoid Patpong area touts entirely. If you must, confirm all prices in writing before entering and carry only cash you're willing to lose.

scams.name: Taxi meter refusal
scams.description: Taxi drivers refuse to use the meter and quote inflated flat rates, especially from airports and tourist areas. Rates can be 3-5x the metered fare.
scams.avoidance: Always insist on the meter ('meter, krap/ka'). If refused, exit and find another taxi. Use Grab app for fixed-price rides. At airports, use the official taxi queue.

connectivity.simOptions: Tourist SIM cards from AIS, DTAC, or TrueMove available at airports and 7-Elevens ($5-15 for 7-30 days with 15-100GB). eSIM via Airalo or Holafly ($5-12). AIS is the best coverage nationwide.
connectivity.wifiAvailability: Free WiFi widely available at hotels, cafes, restaurants, malls, and 7-Elevens. Quality is generally good in cities. Patchy on islands and rural areas.
connectivity.bestOption: Airport SIM card from AIS (best coverage) or TrueMove at Suvarnabhumi/Don Mueang arrivals. eSIM if your phone supports it — activate before arrival.

cultural.tipping: Not traditionally expected but appreciated. 20-50 baht for good restaurant service. Round up taxi fares. Hotel porters 20-50 baht per bag. Spa/massage 50-100 baht.
cultural.dressCode: Cover shoulders and knees at temples (required — many temples provide wraps). Remove shoes before entering temples and homes. Avoid wearing black to temples.
cultural.greetings: Wai greeting (palms together, slight bow) is the standard. Higher hands = more respect. Don't wai to children or service staff. A smile goes a long way — Thailand is the 'Land of Smiles.'
taboos: Touching someone's head (highest part of body, considered sacred)
Pointing feet at people or Buddha images (feet are lowest/dirtiest)
Disrespecting the monarchy (lèse-majesté is a serious criminal offense)
Public displays of anger (losing face)
Stepping on money (has the King's image)
cultural.haggling: Expected at markets, street stalls, and with tuk-tuk drivers. Start at 50-60% of asking price. Not appropriate in malls, restaurants, or shops with fixed prices.

safety.lgbtSafety: Very tolerant culturally. Thailand is one of the most LGBTQ+-friendly countries in Asia. Same-sex marriage legalized in 2024. Bangkok has a vibrant LGBTQ+ scene. Kathoey (transgender women) are culturally visible.
safety.soloFemaleSafety: Generally safe. Exercise normal caution at night, especially on islands and in nightlife areas. Drink spiking occurs — watch your drinks. Full moon parties on Koh Phangan require extra vigilance.
safety.notes: Most tourist crime is petty — bag snatching by motorbikes, pickpocketing in crowded areas. Road safety is a major concern: Thailand has one of the highest road fatality rates in the world. Be extremely cautious on motorbikes.

practical.visaFreeCountries: US citizens: 60 days visa-free (extended from 30 in 2024). UK 60 days. EU 60 days. Australia 60 days.
practical.bestTimeToVisit: November-February (cool, dry season). Avoid May-October (monsoon season, heavy rain). March-April is extremely hot (35-40°C).

medications.generalAdvice: Vietnam restricts medications classified as 'addictive' or 'psychotropic' (including many anxiety, depression, insomnia, and ADHD medications) to a maximum 7-day supply. Carry a signed doctor's letter listing your name, medication names, dosages, and the quantity needed for your trip. Contact the Vietnamese Embassy before travel if you need to bring more than 7 days' supply. Drug penalties are extremely severe — the death penalty may apply for trafficking — and police conduct random drug testing at nightlife venues and private residences.

scams.name: The Tinder Honeytrap Scam
scams.description: You match with an attractive profile on Tinder and arrange to meet in the Old Quarter. A woman shows up and guides you to a restaurant for dinner, then suggests heading to a nearby nightclub. The restaurant bill comes back outrageously inflated — think $150 for basic food — and the nightclub has a metal shutter that comes down once you're inside, trapping you until you pay hundreds more. This organized ring has been running for 5+ years with an estimated 30-50 victims per night, each losing $100-200.
scams.avoidance: Never follow a Tinder date to a restaurant or club they specifically recommend in the Old Quarter | Agree on a venue yourself beforehand | Read Google Maps reviews of any bar before entering (sort by lowest)

scams.name: The Shoe Repair Shakedown
scams.description: You're walking through the Old Quarter when a friendly man crouches down and starts fixing your shoe — maybe he points out a broken sole or loose strap. Before you can say anything, he's already glued it and demands an enormous fee. When you protest, he gets aggressive and refuses to give your shoe back until you pay. This quick-hands hustle catches tourists totally off guard.
scams.avoidance: Keep walking if anyone crouches near your feet | Never let anyone touch your belongings without discussing a price first

scams.name: The Donut/Street Food Bait
scams.description: A woman carrying a basket of donuts or snacks on a shoulder pole approaches and hands you one to try. Once you've taken a bite, she demands a wildly inflated price — sometimes forcing you to pay for the whole basket. If you refuse, she causes a scene, drawing a crowd and relying on your embarrassment to extract payment.
scams.avoidance: Don't accept any food or items handed to you on the street | If something is pressed into your hands, hand it back immediately without tasting

scams.name: The Cyclo Tourist Price
scams.description: You hop on a cyclo (bicycle rickshaw) for a scenic ride through the Old Quarter and agree on a price — say 50,000 dong. After the ride, the driver demands 10x that amount, claiming the price was per minute or that you misunderstood. He may grab your bag or block your path while demanding payment, knowing you probably don't want a public confrontation.
scams.avoidance: Always agree on a total price, route, and duration before getting in | Write the agreed price down and show the driver | Consider using Grab (ride-hailing app) instead

scams.name: The Fake Tour Package
scams.description: You book a Halong Bay cruise or overnight tour through a budget travel agency near your hotel. The pictures show beautiful boats and private cabins. When you arrive at the dock, you're herded onto a completely different, far cheaper vessel than advertised. Complaints go nowhere and refunds are impossible — you're stuck on the boat for two days.
scams.avoidance: Book Halong Bay tours through verified operators on TripAdvisor | Ask for the exact vessel name and look it up before paying | Read recent reviews from the past 2-3 months

scams.name: The Taxi Meter Trick
scams.description: You grab what looks like a legitimate taxi from the airport or hotel, and the meter is running — great. But when you arrive, the fare is staggering. The driver either had the meter running on a higher tariff setting, or the meter itself was tampered. Some drivers refuse to turn on the meter at all and then demand a huge flat fee at the destination.
scams.avoidance: Use Grab (Vietnam's Uber equivalent) — fixed price before you get in | If taking a taxi, only use Mai Linh or Vinasun green taxis with verifiable meters

scams.name: Motorbike Bag Snatching
scams.description: You're walking along a busy street in District 1 with your bag over one shoulder or your phone in your hand when a motorbike comes up from behind and the passenger grabs your belongings in one swift movement. It's fast, violent, and sometimes causes injury if the bag strap doesn't break. Ben Thanh Market area and tourist walking streets are prime targets, especially at night.
scams.avoidance: Always wear bags across your body with the bag on the side away from traffic | Keep your phone in your pocket when walking — use it in cafes | Walk with your bag on the building side, not the road side

scams.name: Xe Ôm Price Bait-and-Switch
scams.description: A motorbike taxi driver quotes you an attractively cheap price to your destination — maybe 20,000 VND. You hop on and he takes you on a confusing route through narrow alleys. Upon arrival, he demands 200,000 VND, claiming you misunderstood, the price was per kilometer, or the 'tourist rate' is different. You're far from home and he has your luggage on the bike.
scams.avoidance: Use Grab for all motorbike and car transport in Ho Chi Minh City — price is fixed upfront | If using informal xe ôm, agree on price in writing (show on phone calculator) before riding | Never let a driver put your luggage in a separate container you can't access

scams.name: Cyclo Overcharging
scams.description: A friendly cyclo (bicycle rickshaw) driver offers you a 30-minute city tour for what seems like a very reasonable price. You agree and enjoy the ride. At the end, the driver pulls out a price list that says the price is per person — you assumed it was for the whole ride — and if you're a couple, the charge is now doubled. He then adds extra charges for 'photo stops' you made along the way.
scams.avoidance: Always confirm 'total price' explicitly for the whole agreed route | Get it written on paper with the driver's signature if possible | 30-minute District 1 cyclo tour should be roughly 100,000-150,000 VND total

scams.name: Shoe Shine Ambush
scams.description: A young boy or man near you suddenly bends down and starts polishing your shoes before you can protest. Within seconds he's applied polish and is buffing away. You try to stop him but he insists he's almost done. When finished, he demands $10-20 for the unsolicited service. This escalates quickly if you don't pay, with shouting that draws attention.
scams.avoidance: Keep moving and say 'no' firmly if anyone approaches your feet | If it happens, offer 20,000-30,000 VND maximum — that's a fair local price | Wear trainers or sandals to make you a less attractive target for this scam

scams.name: Fake Tourist Information Office
scams.description: You spot what looks like an official tourist information office near your hotel. Inside, friendly staff offer to book tours, transport, and tickets on your behalf. The prices seem official and reasonable. But the tours they sell are overpriced, often don't match the description, or the commission goes entirely to the 'office' with no added value. Some also upsell travel insurance or visas that aren't legitimate.
scams.avoidance: The official tourist info center is at 39 Le Thanh Ton Street — check the government website | Book tours through your hotel or reputable online platforms | For official government services (visas, etc.), only use immigration.gov.vn

scams.name: Counterfeit Cash Change
scams.description: You pay for food or shopping with a larger VND note and receive change, but mixed in are badly printed counterfeit bills. Vietnamese currency is unfamiliar to most tourists, especially in dim restaurant lighting, making counterfeits hard to spot in the moment. Some street vendors also give short change knowing tourists can't quickly do VND mental arithmetic.
scams.avoidance: Exchange money at official banks or hotel desks — never on the street | Learn what authentic VND feels like — run your thumb over the holographic strip | Use cashless payment where possible, or pay with exact change to avoid the issue

connectivity.simOptions: Prepaid SIMs from Viettel (best coverage), Vinaphone, or Mobifone at airports and convenience stores. ~100,000-200,000 VND for 5-20GB (~$4-8 USD). eSIM via Airalo or Holafly from $4 USD. Registration requires passport.
connectivity.wifiAvailability: Excellent WiFi in hotels, cafes, and restaurants throughout Vietnam. Vietnam has very fast internet speeds. Free WiFi at most coffee shops (Vietnam has a famous cafe culture).
connectivity.bestOption: Viettel prepaid SIM for best national coverage including rural areas. Buy at Noi Bai (Hanoi) or Tan Son Nhat (Ho Chi Minh City) airport. eSIM from Airalo is excellent for Vietnam.

cultural.tipping: Not traditional but increasingly appreciated in tourist areas. Leave 10-15% at tourist restaurants and bars in Hanoi/Ho Chi Minh City (rarely automatic). Tip tour guides 50,000-100,000 VND/day. Round up taxi fares. Hotel porters: 20,000-50,000 VND.
cultural.dressCode: Modest and conservative, especially in central Vietnam (Hue, Hoi An). Cover shoulders and knees at temples and pagodas. Lightweight, breathable clothing essential for heat/humidity. Long trousers preferred in rural areas.
cultural.greetings: Slight bow with hands together (Buddhist greeting). Handshake acceptable for men in business. Women may not initiate handshake. 'Xin chào' (hello) is universal. Vietnamese is tonal — locals appreciate any attempt. Offer business cards with both hands.
taboos: Touching someone's head (sacred)
Pointing with index finger (point with whole hand)
Losing your temper or showing anger publicly (extreme loss of face)
Patting a child on the head
Taking photographs of military installations
Wearing shoes inside temples, pagodas, and traditional homes
cultural.haggling: Expected and part of the culture at markets, street vendors, and souvenir shops. Start at 50-60% of asking price. Agree on taxi fares before getting in (or insist on the meter). Not in restaurants or fixed-price stores.

safety.lgbtSafety: Relatively tolerant by regional standards. Homosexuality is not illegal. No same-sex marriage recognition. Ho Chi Minh City has a growing LGBTQ+ scene. More conservative in rural/northern areas.
safety.soloFemaleSafety: Generally safe. Bag snatching by motorbike is a known risk in Ho Chi Minh City — hold bags away from the road. Use grab (rideshare app) rather than flagging taxis.
safety.notes: Traffic is the biggest safety hazard — road accidents are common. Cross the street slowly and steadily — motorbikes will flow around you. Bag snatching by motorbike is common in HCMC. Scams in tourist areas (overcharging, fake tours) require vigilance. Use official taxis (Vinasun, Mai Linh) or Grab app.

practical.visaFreeCountries: US citizens: e-Visa required ($25 USD, 90 days, multiple entry). UK citizens: 45-day visa exemption. EU citizens: visa exemption varies by country (France, Germany, Italy: 45 days free).
practical.bestTimeToVisit: October-April for Ho Chi Minh City and Mekong Delta (south). February-April for Central Vietnam (Hoi An, Hue). October-December for Hanoi and northern highlands. Vietnam's diverse climate means there's always somewhere good to visit.

scams.description: Taxi drivers refuse meters and quote inflated prices near airports and tourist areas.
scams.avoidance: Use Blue Bird taxis and insist on the meter. Use Grab/Gojek apps.

connectivity.wifiAvailability: Good WiFi in Bali's tourist areas and major cities. Quality drops significantly outside tourist zones. Most hotels, cafes, and warung (local restaurants) offer WiFi in Bali, Yogyakarta, and Jakarta.

cultural.tipping: Not obligatory but increasingly expected in tourist areas. 10% at restaurants if not included. Tip tour guides Rp 50,000-100,000/day. Round up taxis or tip Rp 5,000-10,000. Gig drivers (Gojek/Grab): tip in-app.
cultural.dressCode: Conservative dress is important, especially outside Bali's tourist areas. Shoulders and knees covered when visiting temples, mosques, and villages. Sarong and sash required at Bali temples (often provided or rented). Beachwear stays at the beach. In Sumatra and Java, dress modestly.
cultural.greetings: Handshake (right hand only — left is considered unclean). Younger people greeting elders: bow slightly or touch elder's hand to forehead. 'Selamat pagi/siang/sore/malam' (Good morning/afternoon/evening/night). Smile is universal and very important.
taboos: Using the left hand for giving/receiving anything, eating, or pointing
Pointing with your index finger (use thumb instead)
Touching someone's head (considered sacred)
Entering a temple or home with shoes on
Public displays of affection beyond hand-holding
Disrespecting Islam, local customs, or the Indonesian flag/national anthem
cultural.haggling: Expected in markets, street stalls, and souvenir shops. Start at 40-50% of the asking price and negotiate to around 60-70%. Not in fixed-price stores or restaurants.

safety.lgbtSafety: Homosexuality is not illegal at the federal level but is banned in Aceh (under Sharia law). Climate is increasingly hostile — avoid public affection. Bali is relatively tolerant but not openly LGBTQ+ friendly.
safety.soloFemaleSafety: Exercise increased caution. Dress modestly outside tourist areas. Harassment can occur. Avoid traveling alone at night in less-touristed areas.
safety.notes: Bali is generally safe for tourists. Main concerns are traffic accidents (scooter/motorbike), scams, and petty theft. Indonesia sits on the 'Ring of Fire' — earthquake and tsunami risk is real. Register with your embassy and follow official advice.

practical.visaFreeCountries: US citizens: 30-day Visa on Arrival ($35 USD) or Bali e-VOA online (recommended). Extendable once for another 30 days. UK and EU citizens: same Visa on Arrival process.

healthcare.costForTourists: Malaysia is a medical tourism hub with high-quality private hospitals at competitive prices. A specialist consultation typically costs $30–$80, and private hospital stays are far cheaper than in Western countries.
healthcare.insuranceAdvice: Travel insurance is recommended to cover private hospital costs, though treatment is affordable by international standards. Ensure your policy covers medical evacuation if you plan to visit remote areas of Borneo.
healthcare.vaccinationsRecommended: Hepatitis A and typhoid are recommended. Hepatitis B, Japanese encephalitis, and rabies vaccines should be considered for longer stays or rural travel in Borneo.
healthcare.hospitalNotes: Private hospitals in Kuala Lumpur, Penang, and Johor Bahru (such as Gleneagles, Sunway Medical, and Prince Court) are excellent with internationally trained doctors. Public hospitals are adequate but overcrowded with long waiting times.

medications.prescriptionRules: Prescriptions from foreign doctors are accepted but may need verification. Antibiotics and controlled substances require Malaysian prescriptions. safety.notes: Malaysia is a popular and generally safe tourist destination with well-developed infrastructure. healthcare.summary: Health & medication guide for Philippines. Emergency numbers (911/117), pharmacy tips, restricted medications, water safety, travel insurance, and vaccination recommendations.
healthcare.costForTourists: Private hospitals in Manila and Cebu provide good care at moderate costs ($50–$150 for consultations). Rural and island healthcare is basic and may require costly medical evacuation for serious conditions.
healthcare.insuranceAdvice: Comprehensive travel insurance with medical evacuation coverage is essential, especially for island-hopping or travel outside major cities where facilities are limited.
healthcare.vaccinationsRecommended: Hepatitis A, typhoid, and routine vaccinations are recommended. Hepatitis B, rabies, and Japanese encephalitis should be considered for longer stays or rural travel. Dengue is a significant risk, especially during rainy season.

soloFemaleSafety.note: Solo female travelers are generally treated warmly but should exercise caution with drink safety, avoid isolated areas at night, and be wary of overly friendly strangers in nightlife areas.

lgbtSafety.note: Filipino culture is relatively tolerant of LGBT people and there is a visible LGBT community, but there are no comprehensive anti-discrimination laws and attitudes vary significantly by region.

safety.naturalDisasters: The Philippines is one of the world's most disaster-prone countries, experiencing approximately 20 typhoons annually (peak season June–November), along with earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and flooding. Travelers should monitor PAGASA weather bulletins and have contingency plans.
safety.pettyCrime: Pickpocketing, bag-snatching, and scams are very common in Manila and other cities, particularly in crowded markets, jeepneys, and tourist areas. Be vigilant with belongings and avoid carrying large amounts of cash.
safety.violentCrime: Armed robbery, kidnapping, and violent crime occur, particularly in Mindanao and the Sulu Archipelago. In Manila and Cebu, express kidnappings and opportunistic armed robberies have been reported, especially targeting those displaying wealth.
safety.notes: Most tourist areas like Boracay, Palawan, and Cebu's resorts are reasonably safe and well-managed. The FCDO and US State Department advise against all travel to western and central Mindanao, the Sulu Archipelago, and the south of the Zamboanga Peninsula due to terrorism and kidnapping risks. Corruption and scams involving police or officials occasionally affect tourists.

practical.visaFreeCountries: US citizens: 30 days visa-free (extendable). UK, EU, Australia also 30 days. Can extend up to 36 months at immigration offices.
practical.bestTimeToVisit: November-May (dry season). December-February best weather. Avoid June-October (typhoon season, especially August-October).

travelAdvisoryUK.summary: Most visits to Cambodia are trouble-free. Be alert to petty theft and bag snatching. Avoid walking alone at night in cities. Exercise caution in areas with unexploded ordnance.

healthcare.systemType: Underdeveloped public system; private hospitals in Phnom Penh and Siem Reap recommended for tourists
healthcare.costForTourists: Private clinic visit $30-80. Emergency care at international clinics $100-400. Serious conditions require evacuation to Bangkok (approx. $15,000-50,000). Hospital stay at private facilities $200-600/night.
healthcare.pharmacyAccess: Pharmacies common in cities. Quality varies — counterfeit medications exist. Stick to reputable pharmacies in tourist areas.
healthcare.hospitalNotes: Calmette Hospital and Royal Phnom Penh Hospital serve emergencies. For serious conditions, medical evacuation to Bangkok or Singapore is strongly recommended.
healthcare.insuranceAdvice: Comprehensive travel insurance including emergency medical evacuation is essential. Medical facilities outside Phnom Penh are severely limited.

pharmacy.hours: Pharmacies are widely available in Phnom Penh and Siem Reap, typically open 8am-9pm. Rural areas have fewer pharmacies with limited stock. Look for 'Pharmacy' or 'Store' signs — many medications are sold in general stores.
pharmacy.tips: Many medications available by prescription in Western countries are available OTC in Cambodia. Antibiotics, pain medications, and other drugs can often be purchased without prescription. Quality of medications varies — counterfeits are a known problem. Stick to reputable pharmacies in cities.

vaccinations.notes: No mandatory vaccinations for most travelers. However, Hepatitis A, Hepatitis B, Typhoid, and Rabies are strongly recommended due to variable healthcare and food/water safety. Ensure routine vaccinations are current. Consider Japanese Encephalitis vaccination for extended rural stays.

water.notes: Do NOT drink tap water in Cambodia. Bottled water is essential — always drink sealed bottled water. Use bottled or purified water for brushing teeth. Avoid ice in drinks outside reputable establishments.

healthcare.foodSafetyTips: Be very cautious with food. Eat at reputable restaurants. Avoid raw vegetables and salads unless you're confident in the establishment. Peel fruits yourself. Only eat cooked foods served hot. Street food can be risky — only eat from busy, clean-looking stalls. Diarrhea is very common.

travelInsurance.requiredNote: Strongly recommended, and some travel insurance is required for visa-on-arrival for some nationalities. Make sure your insurance covers medical evacuation — critical for serious conditions.
travelInsurance.tips: Medical evacuation to Bangkok costs $10,000-30,000+. This is the single most important coverage. Public hospitals are inadequate for serious conditions. Private clinics are better but still limited. Carry your insurance contact numbers. Phnom Penh has some good private hospitals but serious conditions need evacuation.

healthcare.qualityNotes: Healthcare quality varies dramatically. Phnom Penh and Siem Reap have international clinics with decent care (Royal Phnom Penh Hospital, Sunrise Japan Hospital, Angkor Hospital for Children). Rural areas have very limited facilities. Serious medical conditions require evacuation to Bangkok or Singapore. English is commonly spoken in tourist-oriented medical facilities.

healthcare.summary: Health & medication guide for Singapore. Emergency numbers (995/999), pharmacy tips, restricted medications (strict drug laws), travel insurance, water safety, and vaccination recommendations.
healthcare.costForTourists: Healthcare is world-class but expensive for tourists. A GP visit costs SGD 50-100, while emergency room visits start at SGD 100-300. Hospital stays can run several thousand dollars per day.
healthcare.insuranceAdvice: Comprehensive travel insurance with high medical coverage (at least USD 100,000) is essential, as private hospital costs in Singapore are among the highest in Asia.
healthcare.vaccinationsRecommended: No special vaccinations required for entry. Hepatitis A and typhoid are recommended as precautions. Dengue fever is present, so use mosquito repellent.
healthcare.hospitalNotes: Singapore has world-class hospitals including Mount Elizabeth, Gleneagles, and Raffles Hospital. Public hospitals like Singapore General Hospital also provide excellent care at lower cost.

medications.prescriptionRules: Singapore has strict prescription requirements. Medications prescribed by foreign doctors are NOT automatically accepted — a Singapore doctor may need to re-prescribe. Controlled substances require Singaporean authorization. Some common medications (like certain antihistamines) are available OTC.

restrictedMeds.name: Diazepam (Valium) and benzodiazepines
restrictedMeds.note: Strictly controlled. Requires Singaporean prescription or authorization from the Health Sciences Authority (HSA). Bring your foreign prescription and doctor's letter. Singapore customs is very strict about controlled substances.

restrictedMeds.name: Codeine-containing medications
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled. Small quantities for personal use may be allowed with documentation, but a Singaporean prescription is safer.

restrictedMeds.name: Tramadol
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled opioid. Requires prescription or HSA authorization. Singapore takes a zero-tolerance approach to drug trafficking.

restrictedMeds.name: ADHD medications (Adderall, Ritalin, Vyvanse)
restrictedMeds.note: Strictly controlled. Requires Singaporean prescription or special authorization from HSA. Contact the Singaporean embassy before traveling with ADHD medications. Penalties for unauthorized possession are severe.

restrictedMeds.name: Medical cannabis
restrictedMeds.note: Cannabis is illegal in Singapore — severe penalties including death for trafficking. There are no exceptions. Do not bring any cannabis products, including CBD.

medications.bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter in English listing all medications with generic names. Keep medications in original packaging. For any potentially controlled medications, carry the original prescription and HSA authorization if required. Declare all medications at customs.
medications.generalAdvice: Singapore has extremely strict drug laws — trafficking carries a mandatory death penalty and possession of even small amounts of controlled substances can result in long prison terms. All medications should be in original packaging with a valid prescription. Controlled substances such as opioids, benzodiazepines, and sleeping pills require prior approval from the Health Sciences Authority (HSA) — apply online before travel. Bring no more than 3 months' supply.

controlledSubstances.note: Class C controlled drugs under the Misuse of Drugs Act. Legal with valid prescription. Travelers may bring up to 3 months' supply with doctor's letter and original packaging. HSA approval needed for larger quantities.

Amphetamines are Class A controlled drugs — the most serious category. Adderall is completely banned. Importing ANY quantity can result in severe penalties including caning and lengthy imprisonment. Death penalty applies for trafficking (>15g).
Strictly banned. Cannabis is Class A. CBD products are also prohibited regardless of THC content. Trafficking >500g carries mandatory death penalty. Even trace amounts in urine can lead to charges.

Codeine at low doses is available OTC in some preparations. Stronger opioids are Class A controlled drugs. Travelers should carry prescriptions and keep medications in original packaging. Morphine trafficking >30g carries death penalty.
Available in pharmacies with ID registration. Not a controlled drug but regulated as a precursor. Travelers may bring personal supply in original packaging without special permit.

safety.naturalDisasters: Singapore has very low natural disaster risk. Occasional flash flooding occurs during monsoon season (November-January), and regional haze from Indonesian forest fires can affect air quality.
safety.pettyCrime: Singapore has exceptionally low petty crime rates due to strict law enforcement. Pickpocketing is rare but take standard precautions in crowded tourist areas like Orchard Road.
safety.violentCrime: Violent crime is extremely rare in Singapore. It consistently ranks as one of the safest cities in the world for personal safety.

safety.notes: Singapore is exceptionally safe with strict laws that are rigorously enforced. Be aware that chewing gum, littering, jaywalking, and drug offenses carry heavy penalties. The death penalty applies for drug trafficking.
